## Simple explanation

Git records changes to files over time, allowing developers to review
history, work on separate branches, and combine contributions.

## Technical explanation

Git stores content-addressed snapshots in a repository and represents
history as commits connected by parent relationships. Branches are
movable references to commits. Local repositories can exchange commits
with remotes, and merges or rebases integrate changes.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Version control helps teams review code, configuration, and documentation
changes. Machine-learning projects also need explicit strategies for
versioning large datasets, model artifacts, and experiment metadata,
which are not always suited to ordinary Git storage.

## How it works

Changes are staged, recorded in commits with messages, and shared
through branches and remotes. Teams use review workflows to discuss and
validate proposed changes before integrating them.

## Practical example

A developer can create a branch for a model-evaluation change, commit
the code and test updates, and open a pull request so teammates can
review the differences.

## Common misconceptions

- Git and GitHub are different: Git is the version-control system;
  GitHub is one hosting and collaboration service.
- A commit does not automatically include untracked or unstaged files.
- Git is not designed to efficiently store every large dataset or
  frequently changing model artifact.
